t.3.69.1: Having pointed out to Rāma the way toward the recovery of Sītā, Kabandha, who knew the meaning of things, again spoke words full of sense.
t.3.69.2: O Rāma, this is the auspicious path, where these blossoming trees, delightful to the heart, shine forth, stretching toward the western quarter.
t.3.69.4: Climbing those trees, or else forcibly bringing them down to the ground, you two will go on your way eating fruits that are like nectar.
t.3.69.3: Rose-apple, priyāla and jackfruit trees, plakṣa, banyan and tinduka trees, aśvattha and karṇikāra trees, mango trees, and other trees as well stood there.
t.3.69.5: Wandering through excellent regions, from mountain to mountain and from forest to forest, you two will then reach the lotus lake named Pampā, O heroes.
t.3.69.7: There, O Rāghava, swans, plavas, krauñcas and ospreys, dwelling in the waters of the Pampā, coo with sweet voices.
t.3.69.6: O Rāma, you will come to that lake, free of gravel and not slippery underfoot, with even fords and no moss, its banks covered with fine sand and adorned with lotuses and water-lilies.
t.3.69.8: Those beautiful birds, ignorant of slaughter, do not take fright on seeing men; you two will eat those plump birds, like balls of ghee.
t.3.69.9: There on the Pampā, O Rāghava, O Rāma, the choicest fish, rohitas, vakratuṇḍas and nalamīnas, struck down with arrows...
t.3.69.10: Lakṣmaṇa, filled with devotion to you, will offer you plump fish, stripped of skin and fins, roasted on iron spits, each with only a single bone.
t.3.69.11: As you eat the fish to your heart's content, the water of Pampā amid its heaps of flowers will be yours: lotus-scented, pure, pleasantly cool and wholesome.
t.3.69.12: Then Lakṣmaṇa, drawing up that pure water, gleaming like silver and crystal, will give it to you to drink from a lotus leaf.
t.3.69.13: O best of men, at Pampā you will see stout, handsome boars that make their beds in mountain caves and roam the forest, come down from desire for water and bellowing like bulls.
t.3.69.14: O Rāma, as you wander there in the evening and see the trees adorned with garlands of blossoms and the cool water of Pampā, you will cast off your grief.
t.3.69.15: There, O Rāghava, you will find tilaka and naktamālaka trees laden with flowers, and blooming utpalas and lotuses.
t.3.69.16: No man there would ever put on those garlands; there dwelt the disciples of Mataṅga, sages of deeply composed mind.
t.3.69.17: The drops of sweat that swiftly fell to the earth from the bodies of those who, burning under their burdens, were bringing forest produce for their guru…
t.3.69.18: Those garlands, which sprang up then from the drops of the sages' sweat through the power of their austerities, do not perish, O Rāghava.
t.3.69.19: Even today, O Kākutstha, their attendant, a long-lived ascetic woman named Śabarī, is still seen there.
t.3.69.20: She, ever steadfast in dharma, having seen you, O Rāma, who are like a god and honored by all beings, will go to the world of heaven.
t.3.69.21: Then, O Rāma, keeping to the western shore of the Pampā, you will see, O Kākutstha, that peerless and hidden hermitage.
t.3.69.22: By the ordinance of that sage Mataṃga, the elephants there are unable to enter that hermitage and that forest.
t.3.69.23: In that forest, which resembles Nandana and is like the grove of the gods, teeming with birds of many kinds, you will delight, O Rāma, free from care.
t.3.69.24: In front of Pampā lies Ṛṣyamūka, its trees in bloom, truly very hard to climb and guarded by young elephants. That lofty mountain was fashioned by Brahmā himself in ancient times.
t.3.69.25: O Rāma, a man who sleeps on the summit of that mountain obtains on waking whatever wealth he gains in a dream.
t.3.69.26: But a man of crooked conduct and sinful deeds does not climb it; if he does, the rākṣasas seize him as he sleeps and strike him down right there.
t.3.69.27: And from there too, O Rāma, is heard the great trumpeting of the young elephants that dwell in the Mataṃga forest as they play in the Pampā.
t.3.69.28: Drenched with streams of blood, the mighty elephants, dark as clouds and full of vigour, having clashed together, now roam about, scattered here and there.
t.3.69.29: Having drunk there the water, clear, cool and inexhaustible, those forest-dwelling creatures turn back and plunge again into the woods.
t.3.69.30: O Rāma, on that mountain there shines a great cave, its mouth closed by a rock, O Kākutstha, and entering it is difficult.
t.3.69.31: At the eastern entrance of that cave lies a great lake of cool water, delightful, rich in roots and fruits, and surrounded by trees of many kinds.
t.3.69.32: In that cave dwells Sugrīva together with four monkeys; at times he stays upon the summit of that mountain.
t.3.69.33: Having thus instructed both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the mighty Kabandha, garlanded and radiant with the hue of the sun, shone brightly in the sky.
t.3.69.35: And he said to the two of them, "Go forth for the accomplishment of your purpose." Then Kabandha, having taken leave of the two, who were well pleased, departed.
t.3.69.34: Then Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, ready to set out, spoke these words from close by to the illustrious Kabandha, who stood in the sky: "You may go now."
t.3.69.36: Then Kabandha, having regained that form of his, wrapped in splendour, his body radiant like the sun, stood in the sky, looked down at Rāma and, pointing the way, said to him, "Make friendship."
